t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: What Gazebo Is: The Robot's Proving Ground
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: What Gazebo Is: The Robot's Proving Ground
description: Gazebo is where robots crash safely: a 3D simulator with real physics engines (ODE, Bullet, DART), sensor models that publish like real hardware, and worlds described in SDF files — buildings, terrain, lighting, wind. The modern stack (Ignition, now 'gz') rebuilt the architecture around distributed transport and plugins. Paired with ROS 2, the autonomy stack cannot distinguish sim from reality, which makes Gazebo the gate every behavior must pass before hardware.
key_facts: ROS 2 bridge: sim indistinguishable to the stack

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: SDF: Describing Worlds and Robots
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: SDF: Describing Worlds and Robots
description: SDF (Simulation Description Format) is Gazebo's XML language for everything: robot links, joints, inertias, sensors, and world geometry, lighting, and physics parameters. Writing SDF by hand teaches the physics — every mass and friction coefficient is a modeling decision. The discipline is measured parameters: a robot model with guessed inertias lies to you, and sim-to-real transfer dies on lies. Weigh the parts, measure the friction, then simulate.
key_facts: Every physical parameter is a modeling decision

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Physics Engines: ODE, Bullet, DART
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Physics Engines: ODE, Bullet, DART
description: Gazebo supports multiple physics engines because they trade differently: ODE is the classic default, Bullet handles complex contact well, DART offers accurate articulated dynamics. The engine choice, solver iterations, and time step jointly determine sim fidelity and speed — smaller steps are truer but slower. For contact-rich tasks (manipulation, legged locomotion) the engine settings are the experiment; for open-field driving they barely matter. Know which regime you are in.
key_facts: Time step and iterations set fidelity

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Sensor Models: Lidar, Cameras, IMU
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Sensor Models: Lidar, Cameras, IMU
description: Gazebo's sensor plugins generate the data autonomy consumes: GPU lidar with noise models, cameras with lens distortion, IMUs with bias drift, GPS with dropouts. The noise models are the point — a perfect sensor teaches the stack nothing about reality. Configuring sensor noise from the datasheet (or better, from measurements of the real sensor) is what makes sim transfer work. A stack that survives noisy sim sensors survives the field.
key_facts: GPU lidar, cameras, IMU with noise models

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Your First World: A Robot in a Room
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Your First World: A Robot in a Room
description: The hello-world: spawn a differential-drive robot in a walled room, drive it with teleop, watch the lidar paint the walls in the visualizer. The SDF is a few dozen lines; the lesson is the loop — edit world, run, observe, repeat. From there: add obstacles, add a second robot, script the scenario. Every complex sim is this loop scaled up, and the engineers who iterate fastest learn fastest.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Plugins: Extending the Simulator
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Plugins: Extending the Simulator
description: Gazebo plugins are C++ code that hooks into the sim: model plugins control robots, sensor plugins generate data, world plugins script scenarios (wind gusts, moving obstacles, fault injection). The plugin API is how custom physics, proprietary sensors, and test harnesses join the sim. Well-factored plugins are also how teams share scenarios — the scenario, not just the robot, becomes versioned code.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Distributed Simulation: Many Machines, One World
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Distributed Simulation: Many Machines, One World
description: Big worlds need more than one machine: Gazebo's distributed architecture (especially the Ignition/gz transport) splits simulation across processes and hosts — physics here, sensors there, visualizer elsewhere. This is how city-scale driving sims and swarm scenarios run in real time. The cost is clock synchronization and network determinism; the discipline is measuring the sync error and keeping it below what the experiment can tolerate.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Bridging to ROS 2: Topics In and Out
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Bridging to ROS 2: Topics In and Out
description: Gazebo's ROS 2 bridge is the seam between sim and stack: sensor plugins publish /scan and /camera on the same topics real drivers use, and /cmd_vel subscriptions drive the simulated robot. The bridge handles clock (/clock), TF, and joint states — the full graph. The test that matters is the topic-diff: record the sim's topics and the real robot's topics and confirm the schemas match. When they do, the autonomy stack genuinely cannot tell which world it is in.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Defensive Uses: Testing Autonomy Without Risk
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Defensive Uses: Testing Autonomy Without Risk
description: Gazebo's defensive value is risk-free failure: UGV navigation, EOD manipulator procedures, and convoy behaviors can fail ten thousand times in sim before they touch hardware. Scenario libraries encode the hard cases — sensor degradation, obstacle surprises, communication loss — and every software change replays them. This is how you earn the right to field autonomy: the sim has already seen the failure modes, so the field does not have to be the first.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Headless and CI: Simulation Without Windows
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Headless and CI: Simulation Without Windows
description: Sim does not need a screen: headless Gazebo runs on servers and in CI, executing nightly mission suites and reporting pass/fail. The pattern is sim-in-the-pipeline — every commit flies the missions, and regressions are caught before they reach hardware. Rendering sensors still need GPUs, so CI runners carry them; the economics (a GPU server vs. a crashed prototype) are not close.
key_facts: Sim drift treated as a sim bug

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Debugging: When the Robot Falls Through the Floor
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Debugging: When the Robot Falls Through the Floor
description: Sim debugging has classics: robots falling through floors (collision geometry missing), joints exploding (bad inertias or huge time steps), sensors publishing nothing (topic remapping), and the sim running at 0.2x real time (too much sensor load). The ladder is visualizer first (see the problem), then SDF inspection, then physics settings, then the plugin code. Nine times in ten it is the model, not the engine.
key_facts: Visualizer first, then SDF, then physics

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Sensor Noise: From Datasheet to Model
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Sensor Noise: From Datasheet to Model
description: Transfer lives or dies on noise modeling: take the sensor datasheet's noise density, bias instability, and dropout characteristics and encode them in the plugin parameters — or better, log the real sensor for an hour and fit the model. Then verify: does the sim sensor's statistics match the real one's? This measurement loop is unglamorous and decisive. Teams that skip it get sim that flatters and field performance that disappoints.
key_facts: Fit models from real sensor logs

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Testing: Scenario Coverage as a Metric
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Testing: Scenario Coverage as a Metric
description: Mature sim practice measures coverage: which scenarios ran, which behaviors they exercised, what changed since last run. The scenario library is a test suite, and like any test suite it needs curation — retiring obsolete scenarios, adding ones for field incidents (every field surprise becomes a sim scenario), and tracking flakiness. Coverage of the scenario space is the closest thing autonomy has to 'tested'.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Real-World Pattern: Convoy Behavior Validation
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Real-World Pattern: Convoy Behavior Validation
description: A complete pattern: a three-vehicle convoy behavior — follow distances, obstacle handover, comms-loss fallback — validated across 500 seeded sim runs with injected faults before any vehicle moves. The sim measures minimum separation, mission time, and fallback correctness; the gauntlet gates the field test. What the field test then validates is the sim's fidelity, not the behavior's sanity — that was settled in the thousand runs.

t: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Mastery: The Simulation Engineer's Playbook
title: Gazebo / Ignition Robotics: Mastery: The Simulation Engineer's Playbook
description: Gazebo mastery is physics literacy plus software discipline: SDF fluency, engine tuning, sensor modeling from measurement, scenario architecture, and CI integration. The advanced moves are custom physics plugins, distributed city-scale sims, and sim-to-real transfer research. The mindset: the sim is a scientific instrument — calibrate it, or its answers are decoration.
